Behavioral economics operated off a new assumption, introduced by economic sciences laureate Herbert Simon. His model, called “bounded rationality,” argued that consumers have limited information, limited time, and various psychological constraints that lead them not to the optimal financial choice, but simply one they feel good about. So how do we decide what's good enough? Rather than using logic, behavioral economists say we fall back on heuristics— mental shortcuts for making decisions easier and faster. For example, the anchoring heuristic suggests that the first piece of information you get becomes your baseline for future decision making. Psychologists like Daniel Kahneman thought heuristics predict many consumer choices— which means they can be manipulated to control them.
